rounds.title: Perfectly normal office lighting
rounds.context: A person reads beside an electrical experiment. Judge whether AI created this image.
rounds.alt: A seated person reading near large electrical equipment and bright arcs in a historical photograph.
rounds.explanation: The famous Tesla laboratory publicity photograph dates to December 1899. It is a human-made double exposure: the electrical arcs and Tesla were photographed separately. HUMAN does not mean the scene happened exactly as pictured.
rounds.source: Dickenson V. Alley, Tesla laboratory photograph, December 1899; Commons public-domain-US record. Historical double exposure, resized/re-encoded for this app; no generative edits.
rounds.image_reveal:
Nikola Tesla in his Colorado Springs laboratory — December 1899.
Source: Dickenson V. Alley. Historical double exposure.

rounds.title: The protocol committee got creative
rounds.context: Excerpts from four networking specifications. Judge the original writing.
rounds.body:
The bandwidth is limited to the leg length. A typical MTU is 256 milligrams. Some datagram padding may be needed.

[...]

The carriers may sleep while enqueued.
[...]
Packets MAY be marked for deletion using RED paint while enqueued.

[...]

There is evidence that some carriers have a propensity to eat other carriers and then carry the eaten payloads.

[...]

No options were given for decaffeinated coffee. What's the point?
[...]
The resulting entity body MAY be short and stout.
rounds.explanation: These are unchanged excerpts from four human-written April Fools RFCs: 1149, 2549, 6214 and 2324. Marked omissions separate excerpts; their absurdity is intentional.
rounds.source: RFC 1149 (D. Waitzman, 1990), 2549 (D. Waitzman, 1999), 6214 (B. Carpenter and R. Hinden, 2011), and 2324 (L. Masinter, 1998). All published April 1. Exact English excerpts, at most 25 words per RFC, with marked omissions. Individual URLs and excerpt mapping in ContentSources.md.

rounds.title: The printer has been promoted
rounds.body:
At 09:14, the office printer was elected primary database server after reporting the best uptime in the building.

The migration initially went well. Every transaction was acknowledged, stapled and placed in the output tray. Unfortunately, our backup strategy depended on someone remembering to buy paper.

At 10:02, a jam caused the entire finance department to become read-only. The on-call engineer resolved the incident by opening Tray 2 and gently reassuring the printer.

Action items: purchase toner, add a second printer for redundancy, and stop describing the shredder as our data-retention policy.
rounds.explanation: Original AI-written comic incident report. It turns ordinary printer problems into a database outage; it is not a real company postmortem.
rounds.source: Original AI-written English tech satire created for this game, October 4, 2026. No external quotation or real incident claimed.

rounds.title: The aerospace GraphRAG handover
rounds.alt: An anonymized Teams chat about an aerospace GraphRAG pipeline and a technical PDF attachment.
rounds.context: Judge the second message in the conversation.
rounds.explanation: AI wrote the incorrect validation reply. The first message describes document processing, a Neo4j knowledge graph and hybrid retrieval for grounded answers. The reply invents aircraft control, propulsion switching and automatic repair approval. This is a fictional English reconstruction inspired by the presenter's internship topics, not a transcript or claim about an actual colleague.
rounds.source: Original AI-written fictional Teams reply based on the presenter-provided aerospace GraphRAG internship topics. MinerU/DocLing processing, Neo4j entities/relations/ontologies, Microsoft GraphRAG, LightRAG, RAGAnything, vector/text indexing and hybrid retrieval appear in the request. No employer or real employee is depicted; PDF attachment and anonymized profiles are fictional. Existing Microsoft Teams UI reconstruction retained.

rounds.title: A bug report with physical evidence
rounds.alt: A handwritten engineering logbook page with an insect taped beside an entry.
rounds.explanation: A moth was recorded in the Harvard Mark II logbook on September 9, 1947. This is a human-made photograph of the actual logbook, not generated imagery. The engineering term bug already existed.
rounds.source: U.S. Navy / Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren, photograph of the Harvard Mark II logbook. Public-domain U.S. federal government image, resized and re-encoded without generative edits. Correct logbook date September 9, 1947; some legacy photo metadata incorrectly says 1945.

Moth taped into the Harvard Mark II logbook — September 9, 1947.
Source: U.S. Navy / Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren.
